notes.27.1.1: 27.1: “ut ostensum magis ac philosophis” may instead mean “as has been shown to the magicians and philosophers”. 27.3: “argumentum dispar furoris” is uncertain; taken as a different occasion or pretext for the frenzy.

nodes.text: There are spirits, impure and wandering, weighed down from their heavenly vigour by earthly stains and desires. These spirits, then, after they lost the simplicity of their substance, burdened and sunk in vices, do not cease, as a consolation for their own calamity, being lost already, to bring others to ruin; being depraved, to pour in the error of depravity; and, being estranged from God, to separate [others] from God by introducing depraved religions.

That these spirits are demons the poets know, the philosophers discuss, and Socrates knew, who at the nod and judgement of the demon that sat beside him would either decline undertakings or pursue them.

The magicians too not only know the demons, but whatever wonder they play at, they do through demons: it is with the demons breathing on them and pouring into them that they produce illusions, making what does not exist be seen, or what exists not be seen.

Hostanes, the foremost of those magicians both in eloquence and in practice, both honours the true God with the majesty that is his due, and knows that angels, that is, ministers and messengers, guard the throne of God and stand by to venerate him, so that, terrified, they tremble at the very nod and countenance of the Lord. He also made known that demons are earthly, wandering, enemies of humanity.

These impure spirits, then — demons, as the magicians and philosophers have shown — lurk beneath consecrated statues and images, and by their breath acquire the authority of a deity as if present, while at times they inspire seers, while they linger in shrines, while they sometimes animate the fibres of entrails, steer the flights of birds, govern lots, and produce oracles wrapped in many falsehoods.

For they are both deceived and deceivers, since they do not know the pure truth, and what they do know they do not confess, to their own ruin. Thus they weigh [men] down from heaven and call them away from the true God to material things; they disturb life, make sleep restless; creeping secretly into bodies too, as fine spirits, they contrive diseases, terrify minds, twist limbs, so as to force [people] to worship them, so that, fattened on the reek of altars or on sacrifices of cattle, they may seem, by loosening what they had bound tight, to have cured them.

From this source too come the frenzied, whom you see running out into public, themselves seers though without a temple: so they rave, so they revel like Bacchants, so they whirl about. In them too there is the same prompting of a demon, but a different occasion for the frenzy.

From them also come those things that were told to you a little before: that Jupiter demanded the games again through a dream, that Castor and Pollux were seen with their horses, that the boat followed the matron's girdle.
Most of you know that the demons themselves confess all these things about themselves whenever they are driven out of bodies by us with the tortures of our words and the fires of our prayer.

Saturn himself, and Serapis, and Jupiter, and whatever demons you worship, overcome by pain, declare what they are; and surely they do not lie to their own disgrace, especially when some of you are standing by.

Believe them as witnesses when they confess the truth about themselves, that they are demons: for when adjured by the true and only God, unwilling and wretched, they shudder in the bodies and either leap out at once or vanish by degrees, as the faith of the sufferer helps or the grace of the healer breathes upon them. So they flee at close quarters from Christians, whom at a distance, in your gatherings, they used to harass through you.
